audits.claim: Ottoman Turkish is Oghuz-branch Turkic with extensive Arabic/Persian borrowing, written predominantly in an adapted Perso-Arabic script; three prestige languages and three lexical strata are not three scripts, and 'trigraphia' should be reserved for a demonstrated three-script ecology.
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Osmanlı Türkçesi' (Özkan 2007, vol. 33:483-485), opening definition and 'Teşekkülü ve Gelişim Süreci' section
audits.source_excerpt: Oğuz lehçesine dayalı yeni bir dil teşekkül etmiş [...] daha genel olarak Arap harfleriyle yazılmış Türkçe anlaşılmaktadır [...] Tanzimatçılar [...] bunu Arapça, Farsça ve Türkçe’den meydana gelmiş bir dil olarak tanımladılar.
audits.basis: Retrieved article states an Oghuz-based language formed in Anatolia, treats Ottoman Turkish commonly as Turkish written in Arabic letters, and presents the Arabic+Persian+Turkish formula as a Tanzimat-era lexical self-definition rather than a family statement. That is exactly the confusion the entry rejects. No retrieved source uses 'trigraphia' for Ottoman, so the entry's reserve-the-term guidance is consistent with retrieved usage, not contradicted.
audits.access_limit: Article body retrieved; no study dedicated to script terminology was retrieved, so the trigraphia reservation rests on consistency with retrieved usage rather than on a source that names the term.

audits.claim: The standard edition cited for the classification and writing claims, Kerslake 1998 'Ottoman Turkish', exists as cited, and 'Ottoman Turkish' is catalogued as Turkish (Turkic), not as an Arabic/Persian mixed language.
audits.source_locator: Glottolog 5.3 reference record id 549915: citation line and lgcode field
audits.source_excerpt: Kerslake, Celia. 1998. Ottoman Turkish. In Lars Johanson and Éva Csató-Johanson (eds.), The Turkic Languages, 179-202. London & New York: Routledge. [...] lgcode = {Ottoman Turkish = Turkish [tur]}
audits.basis: Record matches the entry's author, year, title, editors, pages and publisher; its language code assigns Ottoman Turkish to Turkish [tur] within Turkic, supporting the entry's family-level, non-creole statement. This is catalogue metadata, not the chapter text.
audits.access_limit: Metadata record only; the 1998 chapter itself was not retrieved, so its internal argument is not audited.

audits.claim: Allographic writing of Turkish (Armeno-Turkish, Karamanlidika) must be dated per corpus, and Strauss's 19th-20th-century study does not set the start date of those corpora.
audits.source_locator: University of Vienna, Cluster of Excellence 'EurAsian Transformations', ATLAS project page, sections 'Mekhitarist Library' and 'Armeno-Turkish Manuscripts, Prints and Newspapers'
audits.source_excerpt: In 1727, he published a grammar of modern Armenian, which is regarded as the earliest printed work in the Turkish language to be produced in Armenian script. [...] between the late 17th and 20th centuries
audits.basis: The institutional project page dates the Armeno-Turkish corpus from the late seventeenth through the twentieth centuries and its earliest print to 1727, so 'date each corpus' is warranted and any implication that allography equals 19th-20th-century publishing is refuted. Dated clarification appended to the entry on 2026-10-17.
audits.access_limit: Project overview page; the digitised corpus and its catalogues were not inspected.

audits.claim: Karamanlidika (Turkish in Greek letters) publishing is datable from the eighteenth century, not only from the nineteenth.
audits.source_locator: Turkish Studies journal article abstract, 'Karamanlı Türklerinin Dil ve Edebiyatları Hakkında Açıklamalı Bibliyografya Denemesi', paragraph on Karamanlidika literature
audits.source_excerpt: The first published text in Karamanlidika literature was emerged in 1718: Gülizar-ı İman-ı Mesihi “Rosegarden of Messianic Beliefs”.
audits.basis: The journal abstract asserts the 1718 first published Karamanlidika text, reports a 1455/56 Turkish text in Greek letters that it does not itself count as Karamanlidika literature, and describes the corpus as largely standard Ottoman Turkish in Greek script. Independently, the retrieved Leiden thesis abstract describes 'the first century of Karamanlidika printing' as an eighteenth-century phenomenon. The 1718 date is recorded as abstract-sourced.
audits.access_limit: Abstracts only; the Cà Foscari EGLL entry PDF and the first-book catalogue record returned HTTP 403, so the 1718 date is not full-text confirmed.

audits.claim: 'Lâle Devri' is a later label, not an eighteenth-century chroniclers' self-designation, and its popularisation is twentieth-century (Özcan 2003).
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Lâle Devri' (Özcan 2003, vol. 27:81-84), opening paragraph of the historical section
audits.source_excerpt: XVIII. yüzyıl Osmanlı kroniklerinde Lâle Devri adı altında bir dönem tanımlaması mevcut değildir. [...] 1913 yılında İkdam gazetesinde tefrika edilen makalenin [...] başlığında kullanılan bu ad Osmanlı tarih literatüründe yaygınlık kazanmış
audits.basis: The retrieved article defines the period name as given later, states that eighteenth-century Ottoman chronicles have no such period designation, credits the term's first use to Yahya Kemal Beyatlı, and attributes its diffusion to Ahmed Refik Altınay's 1913 serialised article and a book two years later. The same article couples the era to dress by recording a fermān against luxury and especially women's excessive adornment.
audits.access_limit: Historical section retrieved; Pala's literary section came in the same fetch but was not audited line by line.

audits.claim: The often-cited 1720s women's-dress decree has conflicting dates in earlier works: 1725, 1726 and 1727 are reported in Quataert (1997), note 45; the disagreement must not be silently resolved.
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Lâle Devri' (Özcan 2003), paragraph on morals, luxury and the fermān; Quataert 1997 (IJMES 29/3:403-425) full text attempted at JSTOR stable/pdf/164587.pdf and the Cambridge Core article page
audits.source_excerpt: özellikle kadınların aşırı süslenmelerinin önlenmesi için bir ferman dahi çıkarılmıştı
audits.basis: An independent retrieved source attests a period fermān on luxury and women's adornment without giving a date, consistent with the entry's caution, but the audited claim is specifically what Quataert's note 45 reports. Quataert's full text was not retrievable, so the 1725/1726/1727 disagreement is neither confirmed nor resolved here; the entry's (to-verify) marker and difficulty warning stand, and no erratum resolves the date.
audits.access_limit: Quataert 1997 full text and notes not accessible (403/paywall on JSTOR and Cambridge Core); search-result snippets were deliberately not treated as confirmation.

audits.claim: Kanun documents and şeriat jurisprudence share vocabulary, quoted authorities and formulae; kanunnames cover fiscal, land, criminal, office and group/provincial matters, and the modern 'secular versus religious law' framing entered later.
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Kanunnâme' (İnalcık 2001, vol. 24:333-337): opening definition, section 5 'Genel Kanunnâmeler', closing paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: Kanunnâmeler kamu hukuku, devlet teşkilâtı, idare, vergi, ceza hukuku ve hisbe [...] alanlarını kapsamaktaydı. [...] müftülerin fetvalarının dahil edilmesidir. [...] resmî kanun kavramı Osmanlı Devleti’ne XIX. yüzyılda girmiştir.
audits.basis: The retrieved article lists the document domains named by the entry, records mufti fetvas being incorporated into later kanunnames — crossing the juristic/sultanic division the entry warns against separating by language — and dates the European sense of statutory 'official law' to the nineteenth century. It also confirms that pre-Ottoman laws (Kayıtbay, Uzun Hasan, Alâüddevle) were kept and recopied as Ottoman kanunnames, matching the entry's counterexample about retained local tax and legal names.
audits.access_limit: Article body retrieved; no sicil register, fetva collection or decree original was collated, so formula-level mixture is supported at the level of the compilations the article describes.

audits.claim: 'Divan' poetry is a conventional scholarly label, and the courtly reading is itself a contested later characterisation, not a neutral description.
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Divan Edebiyatı' (Akün 1994, vol. 9:389-427), section 'Tarifi ve Adlandırılışı'
audits.source_excerpt: “Divan edebiyatı” sözü bunlar arasında en yenisi olduğu kadar en fazla tutulanını da teşkil etmiştir. Mütareke devrinde ortaya çıkan divan edebiyatı tabiri önce Ömer Seyfeddin ve Ali Canip’in kalemlerinde kendini hissettirmeye başlamış
audits.basis: The retrieved section shows the label is the newest of several names, appearing in the Mütareke period and spreading in the early Republic, while rival names such as 'havas edebiyatı, saray veya enderun edebiyatı' are described as reflecting a pejorative mentality. This matches the entry's warning that the label and the court association are scholarly conventions requiring care.
audits.access_limit: Naming/definition sections retrievable within the fetch; the article's remaining pages (up to 427) were not read.

audits.claim: Oğuz/Kayı genealogical claims and the spiritual-sanction story around Osman are retrospective and politically motivated, so the entry's caution against treating them as contemporary testimony is warranted; the moon/tree dream sequence remains redaction-specific (to-verify).
audits.source_locator: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 'Osman I' (İnalcık 2007, vol. 33:443-453; page updated 18.01.2020): paragraphs on the family's descent, the Kayı genealogies, and Edebâli's blessing
audits.source_excerpt: Ailenin menşei ve şeceresi kaynaklarda farklı şekillerde kayıtlıdır. [...] Osman’ın aşireti hakkında kroniklerde aktarılan bilgiler ve soy ağaçları (jenealojiler) hiçbir tarihî esasa dayanmaz. [...] folklorik bir kutsama hikâyesinin ilâvesi [...] beyliğin tanrısal teyidi ve meşrulaştırma gayreti olarak yorumlanmalıdır.
audits.basis: The retrieved article records divergent genealogies, states that chronicle information and genealogies about Osman's tribe rest on no historical basis, and presents the Yazıcıoğlu/Oğuz-Han pedigree as a response to Timurid and Shahrukh superiority claims — a political argument. It treats the Edebâli blessing as a folkloric consecration added for divine confirmation and legitimisation, matching the entry. The article narrates no moon/tree dream, so that sequence stays (to-verify) as the entry marks it.
audits.access_limit: Article body retrieved; no chronicle edition was collated, so the specific dream redaction remains unverified.
